st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The opinion accepts that legal technology can materially outperform conventional methods on suitable tasks, while adding a concrete governance principle: even a generally superior tool should be deployed according to use context, proportionality and responsible-party control rather than mandated as universally best. Its staged discovery orders further illustrate selective, evidence-responsive workflow design.

mo.t: AI privilege: Legal subject matter is insufficient
Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
TAR governance: Reduced review retains legal judgment

kp.k: Courts permit TAR without compelling its adoption
kp.d: Magistrate Judge Andrew J. Peck denied Hyles' request to force the City to use technology assisted review (TAR), or predictive coding, instead of keyword searching. The decision distinguishes judicial permission for a producing party to adopt TAR from compulsion at the requesting party's initiative. Unlike earlier cases discussed in the opinion, this dispute arose before the responding party had incurred substantial search expenditure.
qs: Since the search methodology issue arose in this case before the City spent much, if any, money on searching for responsive ESI, this case squarely raises the issue of whether the requesting party can have the Court force the responding party to use TAR.
Hyles' application to force the City to use TAR is DENIED.

kp.k: Responding parties retain control over discovery technology
kp.d: Peck grounded the decision in Sedona Principle 6, which assigns responding parties primary responsibility for selecting procedures and technology for their own electronically stored information. Although he endorsed discovery cooperation and noted the December 1, 2015 amendments' emphasis on it, he rejected cooperation as grounds for imposing TAR.
qs: Responding parties are best situated to evaluate the procedures, methodologies, and technologies appropriate for preserving and producing their own electronically stored information.
Cooperation principles, however, do not give the requesting party, or the Court, the power to force cooperation or to force the responding party to use TAR.

kp.k: Reasonableness and proportionality govern, not technological perfection
kp.d: The opinion allows keyword searching even if TAR might yield a more complete production. Technology choice remains subject to scrutiny of the resulting production: demonstrated deficiencies could require the City to repeat its search. Quoting Sedona Principle 7, the court places the burden of showing inadequate preservation and production on the requesting party seeking to compel discovery.
qs: the standard is not perfection, or using the "best" tool (see 7/18/16 Ltr. at 4), but whether the search results are reasonable and proportional.
If Hyles later demonstrates deficiencies in the City's production, the City may have to re-do its search.
The requesting party has the burden on a motion to compel to show that the responding party's steps to preserve and produce relevant electronically stored information were inadequate.

kp.k: Peck endorses TAR's efficiency, especially continuous active learning
kp.d: Despite refusing compulsion, Peck asserted TAR's general cost and performance advantages over keyword searching. He particularly endorsed continuous active learning (CAL), referring to research studies cited in Rio Tinto rather than presenting new measurements in this opinion. He described CAL as eliminating seed-set and tool-stabilization issues.
qs: Hyles absolutely is correct that in general, TAR is cheaper, more efficient and superior to keyword searching.
To be clear, the Court believes that for most cases today, TAR is the best and most efficient search tool.

That is particularly so, according to research studies (cited in Rio Tinto), where the TAR methodology uses continuous active learning ("CAL"), which eliminates issues about the seed set and stabilizing the TAR tool.

kp.k: Pricing and existing staffing complicate TAR's economic appeal
kp.d: The City opposed TAR on cost grounds and because it doubted the parties could collaborate on a seed set after difficult scope negotiations. Peck acknowledged that some vendors charge more for TAR than keywords and asserted that review-time savings usually offset this premium. He qualified that economic argument here by noting that salaried Corporation Counsel staff would conduct the review internally.
qs: The City declined, both because of cost and concerns that the parties, based on their history of scope negotiations, would not be able to collaborate to develop the seed set for a TAR process.
The Court acknowledges that some vendor pricing models charge more for TAR than for keywords. Usually any such extra cost is more than offset by cost savings in review time.
Here, however, the City indicated that document review will be done in house by salaried staff of Corporation Counsel's Office.

kp.k: Review automation parallels choices about human review staffing
kp.d: Peck quoted Dynamo Holdings to support judicial restraint over discovery workflows. That court analogized the choice between human and computer-assisted review to selecting paralegals, junior attorneys or senior attorneys for paper-document review. Peck adopted this analogy to explain why the court should not dictate TAR use, rather than predicting displacement of those roles.
qs: If our focus were on paper discovery, we would not (for example) be dictating to a party the manner in which it should review documents for responsiveness or privilege, such as whether that review should be done by a paralegal, a junior attorney, or a senior attorney.
Yet that is, in essence, what the parties are asking the Court to consider – whether document review should be done by humans or with the assistance of computers.

kp.k: Widespread adoption might eventually change reasonable discovery practice
kp.d: Peck left open a conditional future change in the standard: sufficiently widespread TAR adoption might make refusal unreasonable. He explicitly stated that this threshold had not been reached as of the August 1, 2016 decision; this was a possibility, not a present requirement or a dated forecast.
qs: There may come a time when TAR is so widely used that it might be unreasonable for a party to decline to use TAR. We are not there yet.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Magistrate Judge Andrew J. Peck claims that technology-assisted review (TAR), or predictive coding, generally makes electronic discovery cheaper and more efficient than keyword searching, with continuous active learning offering particular advantages.
pts.d: Peck describes TAR as generally superior to keyword searching and as the best search tool for most cases at the time of the opinion. He states that continuous active learning (CAL) eliminates issues concerning seed sets and stabilizing the TAR tool. He also acknowledges that some vendors charge more for TAR, while asserting that review-time savings usually more than offset that premium. This source concerns predictive coding for discovery, not generative AI.

pts.k: Peck distinguishes judicial permission to use TAR from an obligation to adopt it: perceived technological superiority does not require its use in this dispute.
pts.d: Peck denies Hyles' request to compel the City to use TAR, including where the methodology dispute arises before substantial search expenditure. He adopts the position that responding parties should choose their search methods, subject to reasonable and proportional results and possible remedial searches if production proves deficient. His endorsement of TAR therefore does not amount to a requirement to use the best available technology.

pts.k: Peck raises the conditional possibility that widespread TAR adoption could eventually make refusal to use it unreasonable.
pts.d: This is a qualified future possibility, not a prediction of inevitable adoption or a present legal obligation. Peck explicitly says that the threshold had not been reached when the opinion was issued.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Peck relies on prior discovery decisions, research referenced through Rio Tinto, party submissions, and procedural authorities; the opinion supplies no numerical performance comparison.
pts.d: For TAR's efficiency and CAL advantages, Peck references Hyles' submissions and research studies cited in Rio Tinto, without reproducing study methods, results, or quantified savings. He traces judicial acceptance through his decisions in William A. Gross, Da Silva Moore, and Rio Tinto, and cites subsequent international approvals. For the responding party's choice of methodology, he relies principally on Sedona Principle 6, with supporting discussion of Dynamo Holdings and the reasonable-and-proportional standard under Rule 26(g)(1)(B). These are distinct evidence bases: legal approval does not itself quantify efficiency. The possible future obligation is offered without an adoption forecast or empirical threshold.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims describe discovery practice as of August 1, 2016, with qualified efficiency benefits and an undated, adoption-dependent future possibility.
pts.d: Peck's present-tense endorsement applies to 'most cases,' not all cases. Higher vendor charges and the City's use of salaried internal reviewers qualify the cost discussion. The City also reported concerns about collaborating on a TAR seed set. The refusal to compel TAR concerns the current stage of this dispute and leaves open intervention if later production deficiencies are demonstrated. No date or measurable adoption threshold is provided for the suggestion that declining TAR might eventually become unreasonable.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The direct stakeholders are responding litigants and their review teams, requesting litigants, discovery vendors, and courts supervising electronic discovery.
pts.d: Responding parties may benefit from lower review time and costs but retain methodological choice subject to production adequacy. Here, the affected review team consists of salaried staff in the City's Corporation Counsel's Office, rather than an outside law firm billing review hours. Requesting parties may seek more complete production but cannot compel TAR merely because it is considered superior; they can subsequently demonstrate deficiencies. Vendor pricing affects adoption economics. Courts permit TAR and assess discovery adequacy without necessarily dictating the technology used. The opinion makes no claim about profession-wide employment losses or law-firm staffing changes.
